world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: word stress is assigned individually to syllables practically regardless of what precedes or follows. The basic stress rule for King Island Inupiaq is that the non-final closed syllables and all long vowels—including diphthongs and vowel clusters, which are phonetically long—receive stress. Thus, áiviq 'walrus', íglu 'sod or rock house', and Inúktuyúuq, a personal name. Whereas long vowels (aa, ii, and uu) and diphthongs (ai [e:] and au [o:]) are stressed uniformly throughout their entire quantity, vowel clusters (iu, ui, ia, ua) receive stress on their second member, e.g. puítuq 'it is swollen', except in a word-final syllable, e.g. úi 'husband' and niγiřúaq 'one who is eating'.
new_statements.citation: Kaplan, Lawrence D. 1985. Seward Peninsula Inupiaq Consonant Gradation and Its Relationship to Prosody. In Michael Krauss (ed.), Yupik Eskimo Prosodic Systems: Descriptive and Comparative Studies (Alaska Native Language Center Research Papers 7), 191-210. Fairbanks: ANLC.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-culminative, quantity-driven stress: every heavy syllable is stressed -- any non-final syllable closed by a consonant cluster or long (geminate) consonant, and any syllable with a long vowel, diphthong or vowel cluster (final or not). Light open syllables are unstressed; a word consisting only of light syllables plus a final closed syllable has no stressed syllable ('equally stressless') unless Consonant Gradation lengthens a consonant and thereby closes a syllable. Stress is assigned after, and independently of, the alternating strong/weak 'syllable strength' pattern that drives Consonant Gradation; no single primary-stress position is designated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None distinguished; all heavy syllables are described as receiving stress equally, with no primary/secondary ranking. (Kaplan separately notes single consonants become fortis/long after a 'strong' syllable, but stresses this strength is not phonetic stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final closed syllables are not stressed by closure alone (only 'non-final closed syllables'); vowel clusters take stress on their second member except in a word-final syllable, where the first member is stressed (úi, niγiřúaq); Consonant Gradation can feed or bleed stress by closing or opening syllables (iřítuq [iřít:uq]; KI igáyatuq from /ikayuqtuq/). Rule stated for King Island; CG output differs in Diomede, Wales, Qawiaraq but no different stress rule is given for them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on isolated word forms (citation forms with acute accents); explicitly distinguished from the abstract 'syllable strength' governing Consonant Gradation and from Yupik rhythmic stress. No phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted rule is stated explicitly for King Island Inupiaq (Ugiuvak), one sub-dialect of the Bering Strait dialect of Seward Peninsula Inupiaq (nort2945; Glottolog dialect node for King Island is under Bering Strait Inupiatun). Kaplan presents King Island as representative of the Seward Peninsula group and says stress is assigned syllable-by-syllable independently of Consonant Gradation; he does not restate the stress rule separately for Diomede, Wales or Qawiaraq. NB: Glottolog's only 'grammar' for nort2945, Lanz 2010, actually describes the Malimiut Coastal dialect, which is North Alaskan Inupiaq (nort2944), not Seward Peninsula; it also gives no placement rule.

sources.note: p.193 (PDF p.197, verified on page image): word stress in King Island Inupiaq falls on every non-final closed syllable and on every long vowel/diphthong/vowel cluster (clusters stressed on 2nd member except word-finally); stress is assigned per syllable regardless of neighbours, after and independently of Consonant Gradation; words of light open syllables are 'equally stressless'. p.204: SPI 'syllable strength' (not stress) patterns like Unaliq Yupik stress.

sources.citation: Jenness, Diamond. 1927. Notes on the Phonology of the Eskimo Dialect of Cape Prince of Wales, Alaska. International Journal of American Linguistics 4(2/4): 168-180.
sources.note: No stress/accent rule; only remark is that certain reduced vowels are 'modifications of a, e, i and o respectively in unaccented positions' (p.169). Paper is about sound correspondences (lenition) between Wales and North Slope/Canada/Greenland.

sources.note: Section 2.7 'Stress' pp.42-46 (image-only PDF; scanned): describes MALIMIUT (North Alaskan, nort2944) Inupiaq; gives no placement rule ('Rules for the placement of syllable prominence were not a priority'); reports Lanz 2008 acoustic study: F0, intensity, loudness, spectral tilt significant cues of syllable prominence, duration not; quotes Kaplan 2001 that Inuit lacks Yupik-type rhythmic stress and Kaplan 1994b citing Jacobson that Inupiaq 'has no prosody at all' (which Lanz calls dubious).
